items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

“Inside Gaza,” a 72-minute film following four Agence France-Presse (AFP) journalists reporting from Gaza, won the Best Documentary award and an audience award at Montreal’s Cinemania Film Festival on Nov. 14. The film follows the journalists during the first seven months after Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, documenting the risks and difficulties of reporting from a territory largely inaccessible to international media. Directed by Hélène Lam Trong, the documentary draws mainly on footage the journalists shot for AFP and interviews recorded after they left Gaza. AFP Gaza bureau chief Adel Zaanoun accepted the awards in Montreal and dedicated them to journalists killed in the war and those still working there. The film has won other festival awards and is eligible for consideration for the 2027 Oscars.

items.title: [thestar.com] McGill report finds deepfake network spreading false Canada-U.S. trade claims
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A McGill University research centre says a network of nearly 300 TikTok and Instagram accounts has circulated more than 3,201 deepfake videos that drew 22.1 million views over three months. Many focused on Canada’s trade dispute with the United States. One widely viewed false story described a nonexistent 48-hour ultimatum from President Donald Trump and claimed Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by cancelling $8 billion in U.S. defence contracts. It appeared in 161 videos on 129 accounts and drew 5.1 million views. The report says the accounts promote misleading claims from both sides of the trade debate, while the network’s operators and purpose remain unknown. Researchers said posting patterns and some accounts’ Chinese-language settings or registrations in China point to activity outside North America, but they could not firmly attribute the network to anyone. The report says the accounts have not been monetized and could be building an audience for later use, testing a tool or operating on behalf of someone seeking to influence Canadians.

items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A jury at Woolwich Crown Court in London convicted Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, on Nov. 12 of assisting an Iranian intelligence service by conducting surveillance on critics of Tehran in Britain. Sepahvand was also convicted of conduct linked to preparing a violent attack; Manesh was acquitted of that separate charge. A third defendant, Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, was acquitted of all charges. The targets included Iran International journalists Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, a founder of UK Lawyers for Israel, and a media production professional. British prosecutors and counterterrorism police said Sepahvand acted under the direction of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) or intermediaries, and that the men were offered rewards for sending information to contacts in Iran. Iran has repeatedly denied involvement in espionage in Britain. Police described the verdicts as the first convictions of Iranian nationals under Britain’s 2023 National Security Act. The court is due to sentence Sepahvand and Manesh at the Old Bailey on Dec. 17.

Researchers have described Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct pygmy sperm whale whose fossil skull shows the most extreme facial asymmetry documented in a cetacean, and possibly in any mammal. The animal lived in what is now southern Peru between 6.3 million and 5.6 million years ago and was about 2.7 meters long. Both bony nostrils sat on the left side of its skull. Its dense, downward-curving snout and flexible neck suggest it searched for food in shallow seabed sediments. Researchers propose that it used echolocation to locate buried prey; unlike some bottom-feeding marine mammals, it had no facial whiskers or other specialized sensory structures for foraging.

items.title: [nasa.gov] Voyager 1 stops sending science data before one-light-day milestone
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

NASA’s Voyager 1 has stopped sending science and engineering data, though its carrier signal remains detectable, the agency said as it confirmed the spacecraft reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18. Launched in 1977, the probe is now more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) away in interstellar space; its signal took 24 hours to reach Earth. The spacecraft has sent no data since Nov. 14. Engineers are investigating the fault. NASA said a similar interruption in 2023 was traced to an onboard computer, while the current issue may also involve the computer that collects and formats instrument readings. The carrier signal shows the spacecraft is still transmitting and allowed engineers to verify its distance, but it does not provide the missing science readings. Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd said the team remains in contact with the probe. Because signals take a day each way, sending a command and receiving a response now takes about two days, slowing efforts to diagnose the fault and restore the data flow.

items.title: [eos.org] Arctic ice cores trace century-old toxic pollution to Montana mine
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers traced arsenic and other heavy metals preserved in 10 Arctic ice cores to the Anaconda Copper Mine in Montana, linking pollution to a single industrial source thousands of kilometers away. Arsenic levels in some cores reached about 15 times preindustrial levels around 1914, according to the study in Nature Sustainability. By combining ice-core measurements, atmospheric modeling and historical production records, the team estimated that about 50.5 million Americans and 600,000 Canadians were exposed to arsenic levels associated with increased health risks between 1898 and 1918. Pollution-control equipment installed at the smelter in 1919 reduced emissions by roughly 60% to 65%, though the mine continued operating until 1947. Lead researcher Joseph McConnell, a climate and environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, said epidemiologists should investigate the pollution’s potential effects on people.

items.title: [ft.com] UK tribunal orders disclosure of secret Apple data-access notice
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The UK Investigatory Powers Tribunal ruled on Nov. 19 that the government could not keep secret a notice requiring Apple to give authorities access to encrypted customer data. The Home Office acknowledged issuing it. The judges rejected the claim that confirming the notice would harm national security, saying the government had not established that risk. The ruling addresses disclosure, not whether the government has the legal power to make the demand or what technical changes it requires. Those details remain secret, and a substantive hearing is expected in 2027. The dispute began with a January 2025 demand for access to users’ data worldwide, which Britain later withdrew after negotiations with the Trump administration. A second notice, issued in July 2026 and reportedly limited to UK customers, prompted Apple’s renewed challenge. Apple had already stopped offering its Advanced Data Protection encryption feature to new UK users in February 2025.

items.title: [theguardian.com] European-Japanese BepiColombo prepares to enter Mercury orbit after eight years
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The European-Japanese BepiColombo mission is due to enter orbit around Mercury on Nov. 21 after an eight-year journey of about 6 billion miles, becoming only the second mission to orbit the planet. Its two orbiters will investigate Mercury’s surface, interior and magnetic environment, including its unusually large metal core, the origins of its magnetic field and ice in permanently shadowed craters. A propulsion-system problem delayed BepiColombo’s arrival, and reaching Mercury requires careful braking against the Sun’s gravity. The European Mercury Planetary Orbiter will map the surface’s composition and study the interior; Japan’s orbiter will measure the magnetic field and the planet’s thin sodium exosphere. The spacecraft are scheduled to separate on Dec. 9–10, with science operations planned to begin in April 2027.

items.title: [livescience.com] NASA's Swift telescope burns up after nearly 22 years
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered Earth’s atmosphere and burned up over North Sumatra on Nov. 4, ending a nearly 22-year mission. Its observations, including millions of images, remain available for research. A 24-hour ultraviolet exposure of the Andromeda galaxy was assembled from observations made between May and July 2008. NASA said Swift detected about 20,000 ultraviolet sources there, many of them hot stars and star clusters obscured in visible-light views. Swift was designed to turn rapidly toward short-lived cosmic explosions and observe them in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light. It also alerted other observatories so they could follow events before they faded. The U.S. Space Force said Swift reentered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST over North Sumatra. NASA expected most of the spacecraft to burn up, though some pieces may have survived.

The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC) fined Match Group, the owner of dating app Tinder, €11 million on Nov. 13, ruling that Tinder’s “Download My Data” tool failed to give users adequate access to their personal data. The regulator said the tool omitted some data categories without notice and provided other information only in summary form, violating users’ access rights under the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The regulator also reprimanded Match Group and ordered it to bring its data processing into compliance within three months. DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle said tens of thousands of people used the tool during the period under review and that automated access tools must be fair and transparent about the information they provide. Match Group said it would appeal and defended the privacy protections it had built for Tinder users. The regulator’s order also requires the company to change the tool to provide relevant data and identify information it cannot supply for privacy reasons.

Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [Fast Company] Workers are willing to give up higher pay for one thing, new global survey finds
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Time really is money to many workers.

A better salary is no longer the top reason why workers will consider leaving their job in the next year—heck, it didn’t even crack the top three. For the first time since Adecco launched an annual report on the changing world of work, global workers spanning a wide range of industries are making clear that their time is more valuable.

A better work-life balance topped the reasons why workers might quit their current job, according to a survey of more than 40,000 workers in 36 countries conducted by Adecco, a Zurich-based recruitment and consulting agency. But the second and third reasons why workers might switch jobs—seeking out more flexibility and the opportunity to work remotely—also speak to how people are reevaluating how work fits into their lives, and not just the money it provides, according to the report.

At a time when workers are increasingly being asked to operate alongside AI agents or even robots, as the report found, they seemingly want to retain some of their humanity. And organizations that don’t want to see a mass exodus of humans should take note, according to Denis Machuel, CEO of Adecco.

“We cannot simply ask people to keep pace with technology,” Machuel said in a foreword to the report. “We need to build trust and confidence, to adapt, to give people the freedom to learn and experiment, and protect the flexibility and balance they value.”

The survey also highlighted that across seven key indicators, employees generally reported being somewhat less satisfied this year than last. But the biggest decreases were related to flexibility regarding both their working schedule and working location. 

That’s why the report’s findings also speak to the ongoing tension surrounding stricter return-to-office policies, as Machuel told The Guardian.

“Every company that wants to bring people back to the office struggles with actually implementing these measures to their full extent,” he told the outlet. As for companies with a strict policy of five days per week? “It doesn’t work,” he added.

WORKERS WANT AI

As artificial intelligence continues to reshape how people work, employers play a key role in how that plays out. The survey found that when AI tools are well integrated into everyday workflows, workers save time for higher-value work—and they feel less overwhelmed by the technology as a result.

Nearly three-quarters of workers surveyed use AI agents at work, while 14% work alongside robots, the survey found. These “hybrid workers,” as Adecco dubbed them, report feeling far and away more empowered to shape their work going forward. Compared with their non-hybrid counterparts, these hybrid workers were overwhelmingly more likely to say they’re able to perform at their highest level, that their sense of autonomy over their work has increased in the past year, and that they proactively experiment with different ways of using AI at work.

Once again, employers should take note, Machuel says.

“When workers help redesign how work gets done, and receive the training and clarity to adapt, AI creates more value, and change becomes easier to navigate,” he said in a statement. “AI delivers its greatest impact when it happens with people and not to people.”

Drone strikes killed an employee of the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant and a worker at a nearby thermal power station on Monday, Nov. 9, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said. The agency did not say who carried out the attacks. Moscow-appointed plant management blamed Ukrainian forces for the nuclear-plant worker’s death, while Russia and Ukraine have repeatedly accused each other of attacks around the site. The nuclear plant’s six reactors have been shut down since 2022, but safety systems still require electricity. On Nov. 8, the plant lost its sole 330-kilovolt external power line for about 10 hours and used emergency diesel generators for cooling and other safety functions until power returned. The IAEA has maintained a presence at the facility since September 2022. The latest deaths followed the reported killing of another plant employee in a drone attack on Oct. 29. IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi condemned the attacks and called for them to stop. The agency has not publicly assigned responsibility for the strikes.
